from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out=Path('tmp/pdfs'); out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES',len(reader.pages))
print('METADATA',reader.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
    text=page.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    texts.append(f'\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n{text}')
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency bottleneck: the visual prefix consumed by multimodal language models. Combining attention-based selection with token merging gives a simple, modular approach with potential practical impact.

PruMerge+ offers a promising accuracy–compression trade-off. At the reported 25% token retention, the 7B model achieves 57.1 versus 58.2 on TextVQA and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1). Such compression can be valuable without improving benchmark accuracy.

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. Transfer to Video-LLaVA without additional training is encouraging; ActivityNet-QA accuracy increases from 45.3 to 48.3 with PruMerge (Table 3).

Tables 4–6 provide useful evidence that the complete method outperforms simple spatial sampling, and that supplementation and fine-tuning improve performance. The main models and instruction data are attributed, and Appendix A acknowledges compression losses and potential misuse.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not sufficiently establish the distinctive contribution over existing token reduction. Table 4 compares against taking the first N tokens and uniform spatial sampling, but lacks matched-budget attention top-k selection, pooling, and an adaptation of a cited merging method such as ToMe. Table 5 also does not isolate adaptive budgeting from token ranking or include merging alone. Consequently, the advantages specifically attributable to IQR adaptation and the proposed clustering remain uncertain.

Practical acceleration is insufficiently validated. Table 2 explicitly reports roofline estimates for LLM prefill rather than measured execution. It does not establish end-to-end latency, decoding performance, or the overhead of attention extraction, clustering, and variable-length batching. PruMerge+, which provides the strongest accuracy results, lacks corresponding efficiency measurements. The estimates support computational potential but do not establish deployment gains.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 leaves the neighborhood size k unspecified and replaces a selected center with an unnormalized weighted sum of other tokens, whereas the surrounding text describes weighted averaging and supplementation. Attention-head aggregation and LoRA hyperparameters are also unspecified. Moreover, PruMerge+ adds m tokens to m selected tokens, implying approximately 11% retention from the reported 5.5% baseline, rather than Table 1's 25%; its loop and output still reference only m tokens. These discrepancies may be documentation errors, but they prevent reliable reconstruction of the evaluated method.

The strongest performance-preservation claims exceed the evidence. Even after fine-tuning, 7B PruMerge reduces VQAv2 from 78.5 to 72.0, POPE from 85.9 to 76.3, and MME from 1510.7 to 1350.3 (Table 1). These losses can be acceptable for aggressive compression, but do not support 'without compromising' performance. Section 4.1 also incorrectly claims improved POPE performance. PruMerge+ substantially reduces these losses, but at a different compression level that should be clearly distinguished from the headline claim.

Evidence for the adaptive selection rationale remains limited. Attention sparsity and selected-token visualizations do not establish that IQR-selected counts track task-relevant information requirements. A comparison with fixed budgets at equal average token counts, together with retention distributions and representative failures, would better substantiate this central claim.
